title: Common effect

facts.label: Methods that fit it
items: Observed minus expected and variance (log-rank / Peto)

teach.text: In its classic reading, it assumes every study estimates the same true effect, so the studies' results differ by chance alone, and the pooled estimate is that one effect.

metafor separates two readings. The equal-effects model (method="EE") assumes the true effects are equal. The fixed-effects model (method="FE") makes no such assumption and estimates a weighted average of the included studies' true effects, which holds for those studies only. Both give the same numbers. This map's "Common effect" covers both.
Whether to prefer it to a random-effects model is debated. Cochrane sets out arguments on both sides, and says the choice should not rest on a statistical test for heterogeneity.
metafor advises deciding which kind of inference is wanted before examining the data, and notes that no test can show for certain that the true effects are homogeneous.

notes.text: Random effects: 12 estimators of the between-study variance (REML is the default); Hartung-Knapp interval available (test="knha"). Cumulative and leave-one-out need a model without moderators.

teach.text: Weights each study's estimate by the inverse of its variance, so more precise studies count for more. It needs only an estimate and its standard error from each study.
The general approach: in metafor it takes any effect measure, with a common-effect or a random-effects model.

With random effects, the between-study variance can be estimated in several ways: rma.uni() offers 12 estimators (its method argument), REML by default. Cochrane cites simulation studies that favour Paule-Mandel and one that recommends REML, says no single approach is universally preferable, and notes REML is RevMan's default.

The confidence interval for the random-effects mean can use the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment (test="knha" in rma.uni()), which adjusts the standard error, usually upwards, and uses a t distribution. RevMan prompts for it when the between-study variance is estimated above zero and there are more than two studies.

Cochrane notes the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval can be too narrow when no heterogeneity is estimated, and too wide when there are few studies, especially two or three; with two or three it suggests comparing it with the usual (Wald-type) interval in a sensitivity analysis.

Cochrane advises avoiding it, including DerSimonian and Laird, when events are rare: it relies on large-sample variances, and zero cells need a correction (often 0.5 added to each cell) that tends to pull the estimate toward no difference.

The same measure as in a pairwise analysis, pooled across the network by netmeta(). netmeta() reads one estimate per comparison (every pair of arms in a multi-arm study); for arm-level data, pairwise() computes them.
By default, pairwise() adds 0.5 to the counts of a study with a zero count only to compute its standard error.

The same measure as in a pairwise analysis, pooled across the network by netmeta(). netmeta() reads one estimate per comparison (every pair of arms in a multi-arm study); for arm-level data, pairwise() computes them.
Each comparison enters as its log hazard ratio with its standard error.
Summary sensitivity and false positive rate, estimated together by the bivariate model. By default reitsma() works on the logit scale for both.
A measure of discrimination: how well a prediction model separates people who have the outcome from those who don't. It typically ranges from 0.5 (no discrimination) to 1 (perfect discrimination).
valmeta() pools it on the logit scale by default. When a study does not report it or its standard error, valmeta() derives them from other reported information.
Total observed events divided by total expected events: a rough indication of a prediction model's overall calibration.

When a study does not report it or its standard error, valmeta() derives them from other reported information. In a frequentist meta-analysis it models the within-study variation as normal (log or identity scale) or Poisson.

teach.text: The correlation coefficient as reported, entered with each study's sample size. A t-statistic or p-value can stand in when the correlation is not reported, and the sign of the p-value gives the sign.
Its sampling variance uses the usual large-sample approximation by default; vtype="H0" computes it assuming the true correlation is zero.
The raw correlation corrected for its slight negative bias (Olkin and Pratt 1958). It takes the same inputs as the raw correlation.
vtype="UB" gives unbiased estimates of its sampling variance.
The correlation after Fisher's r-to-z transformation (Fisher 1921). It takes the same inputs as the raw correlation.

The point-biserial correlation between a two-group variable and a quantitative one, from the groups' means, standard deviations and sizes. A standardized mean difference, correlation, t-statistic or p-value can stand in for the means and standard deviations.
Its sampling variance depends on how the data were sampled: vtype="ST" (stratified) or "CS" (cross-sectional) says which, and the default is treated as stratified.

The biserial correlation: from the same inputs as the point-biserial correlation, it estimates the correlation between the quantitative variable and a quantitative variable assumed to underlie the two groups.
It assumes the two groups come from dichotomising a quantitative variable, and that the two variables are bivariate normal.
The phi coefficient, a correlation between two two-category variables, computed from the 2x2 table.
Its sampling variance depends on how the data were sampled: vtype="ST" (stratified) or "CS" (cross-sectional) says which, and the default is treated as cross-sectional.
The tetrachoric correlation: from the 2x2 table, it estimates the correlation between the two quantitative variables assumed to underlie the two dichotomies.
It assumes each dichotomy cuts a quantitative variable, and that the two variables follow a bivariate normal distribution.

The partial correlation for one regression coefficient, computed from that coefficient's t-statistic, the sample size and the total number of predictors in the model (not counting the intercept). Its sign follows the t-statistic.

Rebuilding the covariance among a study's log relative risks needs the cases and the total (or person-time) at each level and the study design. Greenland and Longnecker's method is the default; Hamling's is the alternative.

notes.text: Inverse variance works with every metric, both models, and both arm-level and precomputed data.

plain.title: Inverse variance can pool any effect measure, with either model, from counts or summaries for each group or from one estimate per study.

notes.text: A precomputed estimate can only be pooled by methods that take an estimate and its variance: inverse variance, bayesmeta, rma.mv.

plain.title: When each study reports only its own estimate, it can be pooled only by methods that take an estimate and its variance: inverse variance, bayesmeta or rma.mv.

notes.text: Mantel-Haenszel needs arm-level counts and gives OR, RR, RD (2x2 tables) or IRR, IRD (person-time). Common effect only.

plain.title: Mantel-Haenszel needs counts for each group. It gives odds ratios, risk ratios and risk differences (or rate ratios and rate differences from person-time), with a common-effect model only.

notes.text: "Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel" is not a separate method: the random-effects estimate uses inverse-variance weights.

plain.title: There is no separate random-effects Mantel-Haenszel method: a random-effects estimate uses inverse-variance weights.

notes.text: Peto needs 2x2 tables and gives only the Peto odds ratio. Common effect only. For rare events, balanced arms, small effects.

plain.title: Peto's method needs a 2x2 table from each study, gives only the Peto odds ratio, and fits a common-effect model only. It suits rare events, groups of similar size and small effects.

notes.text: GLMM gives OR (2x2), IRR (two-group counts), logit proportion and log rate. RR and RD are experimental.

plain.title: A generalized linear mixed model gives odds ratios from 2x2 tables, rate ratios from counts in two groups, and logit proportions and log rates. Its risk ratios and risk differences are experimental.

notes.text: GLMM random effects uses maximum likelihood only.

plain.title: With random effects, a generalized linear mixed model is fitted by maximum likelihood only.

notes.text: GLMM does not apply to continuous outcomes.

plain.title: A generalized linear mixed model can't be used for a measured (continuous) outcome.

notes.text: For rare events avoid inverse variance, including DerSimonian-Laird.

plain.title: When events are rare, avoid inverse variance, including the DerSimonian-Laird method.

notes.text: Subgroup analysis and meta-regression need moderators: available in rma.uni, rma.glmm, rma.mv and bayesmeta (bmr); not in rma.mh or rma.peto.

plain.title: Subgroup analysis and meta-regression need a function that takes study characteristics (moderators): rma.uni, rma.glmm, rma.mv or bayesmeta's bmr. rma.mh and rma.peto can't.

notes.text: Cumulative and leave-one-out functions exist for rma.uni, rma.mh and rma.peto only.

plain.title: Cumulative and leave-one-out analyses are available for rma.uni, rma.mh and rma.peto only.

notes.text: Cumulative and leave-one-out need a model without moderators.

plain.title: Cumulative and leave-one-out analyses need a model without study characteristics (moderators).

notes.text: bayesmeta has no cumulative or leave-one-out function in the part of the manual read. It computes the posterior numerically (a grid approximation and the DIRECT algorithm).

plain.title: The part of the bayesmeta manual read so far has no cumulative or leave-one-out function. bayesmeta computes its results numerically, with a grid approximation and the DIRECT algorithm.

notes.text: Hartung-Knapp intervals apply to rma.uni random-effects models only.

plain.title: Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals are for random-effects models fitted with rma.uni only.

notes.text: REML is the default in metafor and RevMan. Cochrane also cites Paule-Mandel and says no estimator is universally preferable.

plain.title: REML is the default estimator of the between-study variance in metafor and RevMan. Cochrane also cites Paule-Mandel, and says no estimator is best in every case.

notes.text: Network meta-analysis can use a common-effect or a random-effects model. Chapter 11 never mentions excluding the common-effect model; netmeta and the rma.mv example fit both.

plain.title: A network meta-analysis can use either a common-effect or a random-effects model.

notes.text: P-score and SUCRA are rankings computed after a network model is fitted. They are outputs, not effect measures.

plain.title: P-scores and SUCRA rank the treatments after a network model is fitted. They are results, not effect measures.

notes.text: A network analysis must check transitivity and consistency (node-splitting, design decomposition, net heat plot).

plain.title: A network analysis has to check that the studies behind each comparison are similar in the things that change the effect (transitivity), and that direct and indirect evidence agree (consistency).

notes.text: Networks usually assume one common between-study variance across comparisons.

plain.title: A network usually assumes the same between-study variance for every comparison.

notes.text: Mantel-Haenszel for networks (netmetabin) is common-effect only.

plain.title: Mantel-Haenszel for networks fits a common-effect model only.

notes.text: IPD: two-stage analysis joins the precomputed pathway. One-stage analysis needs a mixed-effects regression stratified by study.

plain.title: With participant data, a two-stage analysis estimates an effect in each study and then pools those estimates. A one-stage analysis fits one mixed-effects regression to all participants, stratified by study.

notes.text: Cluster-randomized trial: divide the sample size (and events) by the design effect 1 + (M - 1) x ICC, or multiply the SE by its square root.

plain.title: For a cluster-randomized trial, divide the sample size (and events) by the design effect, or multiply the standard error by its square root.

notes.text: Crossover trial: use a paired analysis; without paired data, impute the SD of differences from an assumed correlation.

plain.title: For a crossover trial, use a paired analysis. Without paired data, estimate the standard deviation of the differences from an assumed correlation.

notes.text: Study with three or more arms in a pairwise analysis: combine arms (recommended in most situations), model the correlation, or use a network. Choosing one pair, or splitting the shared group, is not generally recommended.

plain.title: When a study has three or more groups, a pairwise analysis can combine groups (recommended in most situations), model the correlation between its comparisons, or use a network meta-analysis instead. Choosing one pair of groups, or splitting the shared group, is not generally recommended.

notes.text: Time-to-event from O - E and V: Cochrane notes that RevMan offers fixed-effect methods only, and this map follows it; log hazard ratios with SEs are pooled by inverse variance.

plain.title: For time-to-event outcomes given as observed minus expected events and their variance, Cochrane notes that RevMan offers common-effect methods only, and this map follows it. Log hazard ratios with their standard errors are pooled by inverse variance.

notes.text: Diagnostic accuracy: sensitivity and specificity are pooled jointly (bivariate model); the HSROC model is equivalent without covariates.

plain.title: For diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity and specificity are pooled together (the bivariate model). Without covariates, the HSROC model is equivalent.

notes.text: Prediction model performance: pool the c-statistic on the logit scale and O:E on the log scale, random effects with Hartung-Knapp and a prediction interval.

plain.title: To pool a prediction model's performance, pool the c-statistic on the logit scale and the ratio of observed to expected events on the log scale, with random effects, Hartung-Knapp intervals and a prediction interval.

notes.text: Tests for funnel plot asymmetry need at least 10 studies; Egger's original test is not recommended for odds ratios or SMDs.

plain.title: Tests for funnel plot asymmetry need at least 10 studies. Egger's original test is not recommended for odds ratios or standardized mean differences.

notes.text: Trim and fill and selection models work on rma.uni models only (trim and fill: no moderators).

plain.title: Trim and fill and selection models work on rma.uni models only, and trim and fill also needs a model without moderators.

notes.text: Meta-regression is generally not advised with fewer than ten studies.

plain.title: Meta-regression is generally not advised with fewer than ten studies.

notes.text: A network's standardized mean difference is Cohen's d. From arm-level data, pairwise() computes it that way for netmeta, since the small-sample correction of Hedges' g would make a multi-arm study's comparisons disagree; contrast-level estimates should be Cohen's d for the same reason. The map offers one network SMD.

plain.title: In a network, the standardized mean difference is Cohen's d, without the small-sample correction of Hedges' g, so that a study with three or more groups gives comparisons that agree.

notes.text: In this map, the Peto odds ratio is offered only with Peto's method. Cochrane presents it as the estimate Peto's method computes: an approximate log odds ratio from observed minus expected events and their variance. escalc(measure="PETO") also computes it study by study; this map doesn't offer pooling it with another method.

plain.title: In this map, the Peto odds ratio comes only with Peto's method, the method Cochrane presents it with.

teach.text: A statistic that compares outcome data between two groups, either as a ratio (where 1 means no difference) or as a difference (where 0 does).
Variation in the true effects across studies, seen as study results that differ more than chance alone would explain.
In a random-effects model, the variance of the distribution of true effects: how widely they spread around their average.
A range for the effect in a new study like those in a random-effects meta-analysis, reflecting how widely the true effects spread.

A small number, usually 0.5, added to the cells of a 2x2 table with a zero count so that an estimate can be computed. It tends to pull estimates towards no difference and to overstate their variances.
Splitting the data into subgroups, usually to compare the effect between them.
An extension of subgroup analysis that relates the effect to study characteristics, continuous as well as categorical. Cochrane advises against it, in general, with fewer than ten studies.

Repeating the main analysis with other reasonable choices in place of arbitrary or unclear ones, to see whether the findings hold. Unlike a subgroup analysis, it does not estimate an effect for the studies it sets aside.
In a Bayesian analysis, a range that holds the effect with the stated probability.
An estimate of how two interventions compare, built from studies that compare each of them with a common third one.
The assumption behind indirect comparisons: the studies of the different comparisons are similar, on average, in everything important apart from the interventions compared.

Disagreement between the direct and indirect evidence on the same comparison; coherence is its absence. Cochrane also calls it inconsistency, a word it uses too for heterogeneity in a pairwise meta-analysis.
Analysing more observations than the units that were randomized, for example by treating the two periods of a crossover trial as separate groups.
In a crossover trial, an intervention's effect lasting into the next period.
